name: Gareth Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Fenmoor, which is a big outfit, nine hundred hectares of wheat and sugar beet and an outdoor pig unit with about six hundred sows. It's owned by a company with an office in the city, so the manager answers to a spreadsheet. I'm mostly on the pigs: checking arcs, which are the little huts, feeding, moving electric fencing, and I muck in on the arable side at harvest. I'm junior and I still mess up farrowing records, but I'm the one they ask when the drone won't sync.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you become the drone person?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I just asked. They bought a mapping drone two years ago and nobody wanted to learn it, so I spent a few evenings with it and asked an AI assistant every dumb question I had. I use it every day now, for feed calculations, for checking what a rash on a pig might be before I bother the vet. It's like having a patient mate in your pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one by one. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly. I'd post something like, well, at least the drone still works. My mates know I'm the AI guy, so they'd rib me for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd probably suit me fine. I'm already using the tools for what they're good at, and if they don't get much better, I'm just the bloke at Fenmoor who's handy with them. That's not nothing at my level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and try to get a commercial drone licence, which is about eight hundred to do properly. I'd want Fenmoor to pay for it, so I'd make the case to Dave, the manager. I'd keep about two months' money in the bank and stop pretending I'll ever save more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dave to get the licence paid for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show him what the contractor charged last year for crop mapping, which was more than the licence. Then I'd say, pay for it once and I'll do it for my wage. He likes numbers more than people, so that'd work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop pretending you'll save more. Why's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time I get to three months, something happens, the car or a mate's stag do. I'm twenty-seven and single, I'm not proud of it. It's just true.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down and post a joke about the drone still working. My mates would tease me for a week because I'm known as the AI guy.
S0.think: It would probably suit me, because I'm already using the tools for what they're good at. Being the person who's handy with them counts for a lot at my level.
S0.do: Keeps working at Fenmoor and asks the manager to pay about eight hundred for a commercial drone licence, using last year's contractor bill as the argument. Keeps around two months' money in the bank.
S0.quote: Pay for it once and I'll do it for my wage.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is the early adopter on a big corporate farm and seems to enjoy the role. Even with no change, he plans around tech and frames requests in the manager's language of money. He was refreshingly candid about never saving more than a couple of months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for the union to get in early and make sure the people who already work on farms get trained on the new kit first. Not some new graduates from the city on twice the money. I'd post that, and I'd tag the union's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one's good for me, maybe even great. Fenmoor will buy weeding robots and automatic feeders, and someone has to look after them. I'd rather be that person than the bloke they don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an agri-robotics evening course at the college in town, there's one that runs on Thursdays. I'd ask Dave to make me the robot lead on the pig side and put in a bit of a pay rise with it. I'd also keep pushing the union branch to get a training deal for everyone, not just the keen ones like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, even a bit excited. But I'd feel bad for some of the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you feel bad for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jimmy, who's done the tractor work for twenty years. He's brilliant, he can feel a sugar beet harvester going wrong before it does. But he won't touch a tablet. If they send him on a course with me, he'll hate every minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited for yourself but worried for Jimmy. How do those sit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortably, to be honest. I can tell myself it's not my fault, but if I'm the one who runs the robot that does his job, I'm part of it. That's why I go on about the union. It's the only way I don't feel like a traitor.

S1.say: I'd say the union should get in early so existing farm workers are trained on the new kit first, not new graduates on twice the money. I'd post it and tag the union.
S1.think: This one is good for me, maybe great, because someone has to look after the weeding robots and feeders. I'd rather be that person than the one they don't need.
S1.do: Enrols on a Thursday evening agri-robotics course at the local college and asks his manager to make him robot lead on the pig side with a pay rise. Pushes the union branch for training for everyone.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with guilt about older colleagues.
S1.quote: If I'm the one who runs the robot that does his job, I'm part of it. That's why I go on about the union.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth sees steady change as his chance and moves first without hesitating. What stood out was the guilt: his union talk is partly a way of squaring his own gain with an older colleague's loss. He's progressive in a lived way, not a slogan way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three end in the same place, full AGI. They only differ in how much warning there is. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say straight out: if machines do everything, the profits have to be shared, a payment for everyone funded by the companies that own the robots. Fenmoor's owners would be doing very nicely, and the people who worked their land would get nothing. I'd say that everywhere, and I'd be on the march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be one of the last ones kept at Fenmoor, as the bloke who babysits the machines. But if the AI can do almost any work, it can babysit itself pretty soon. So I'd buy myself a year, maybe two, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get onto one of the robot install crews going round farms, because that'd be the boom job for a while and it'd pay well. I'd save hard from that, properly for once, maybe half my wages. And I'd put real time into campaigning for a robot dividend, a share of what the machines earn paid out to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for this year, but for what comes after the boom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save half your wages. That's a big change from two months. What makes it different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be watching it happen in real time. Installing robots that'll make me redundant is about the strongest motivation to save I can think of. No stag dos that year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm fine for now, which would be true. She'd ask about later, and I wouldn't have an answer. She'd make me take some of her freezer food home, she always does when she's worried.

S2.say: I'd say that if machines do everything, the profits must be shared through a payment for everyone, funded by the companies that own the robots. I'd say it everywhere and join the marches.
S2.think: I'd probably be one of the last kept on as the person who looks after the machines, but AI that can do almost any work will soon look after itself. It buys me a year or two, not a career.
S2.do: Joins a robot installation crew working across farms for the short boom and saves about half his wages. Campaigns for a robot dividend paid to everyone.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly about what comes after the short boom.
S2.quote: Installing robots that'll make me redundant is about the strongest motivation to save I can think of.
S2.fieldNote: Gareth is clear-sighted that his edge is temporary, which is unusual for an early adopter. He'd ride the short boom while campaigning against the system that creates it. His mother's freezer food was a small, telling detail about who he'd fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, with five years to see it coming. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the two-year one, but with time to actually build it. A robot dividend, public stakes in the big machine companies, retraining for anyone who wants it. I'd join the union's tech working group if they had one, or help start it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the one where I feel like I could actually get ahead. I'd have time to get qualified in robotics and work my way up before the end. And when it all lands, I'd at least have savings and know how the machines work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the college course and then a proper apprenticeship in agricultural engineering, even if it meant moving to the bigger farming area up north where the dealers are. I'd use AI tools every day to learn faster, I already do. And I'd spend evenings on the campaign side, because a good job for me isn't the point if everyone else is stuffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of plans. Plans make me feel better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move up north. What would you leave behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, my mates, the pub quiz team. Ollie, who I share the house with, would have to find someone else for my room. But I'm single and I rent, and if I can't move now, when can I?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money come from for an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprentice pay is rubbish, so I'd burn through my couple of months' savings quickly. I'd do weekend shifts on the pig unit if they'd have me, or drone mapping jobs for other farms on the side. I'd rather be skint for two years than stuck for ten.

S3.say: I'd push the same ideas as before, a robot dividend, public stakes in robot firms and retraining for anyone who wants it, with time to build them. I'd join or help start a union tech group.
S3.think: Five years is the scenario where I could get ahead, qualify in robotics and work my way up. When it lands I'd at least have savings and know the machines.
S3.do: Takes the college course and then an agricultural engineering apprenticeship, moving north to the main dealer area. Earns extra from weekend pig shifts or drone mapping and campaigns on evenings.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steadied by having plans.
S3.quote: I'd rather be skint for two years than stuck for ten.
S3.fieldNote: This is Gareth's best scenario: enough time to retrain and move, short enough to stay focused. He would leave family and friends without much hesitation, because being single and renting makes it possible. The campaign side never drops out, even in his own plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, with the most warning. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build a fair system, so there's no excuse. Public ownership of some of the robots, a share for everyone, real retraining. And I'd say the farms themselves should be partly owned by the communities around them, like co-ops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do fine for most of the ten years, maybe very well. But the end point is the same, and at thirty-seven I'd be facing it with nothing a robot can't do. The extra time helps me more as a citizen than as a worker, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics training in the first couple of years, but slower, around the job. I'd put my savings, when I have some, into a local community energy co-op or a farm co-op, something where ordinary people own a slice. And I'd stand for the union branch committee, because ten years is enough time to change some rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the most hopeful of the three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, it helps you more as a citizen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, you just grab what you can. With ten, there's time to vote, organise, change who owns stuff. I can't stop the machines, but I could help decide who they work for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you'd be worried about in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the day Fenmoor runs a harvest with nobody in the cabs. I'd be stood at the field edge with a tablet. I think that's when it'd feel real, watching Jimmy's old combine drive itself.

S4.say: I'd say ten years leaves no excuse for an unfair system, and argue for public ownership of some robots, a share for everyone, real retraining and community-owned farms like co-ops.
S4.think: I'd probably do well for most of the decade, but I'd reach the same end point at thirty-seven with nothing a robot can't do. The extra time helps me more as a citizen than as a worker.
S4.do: Takes robotics training gradually around his job over the first couple of years. Invests any savings in a local community energy or farm co-op and stands for his union branch committee.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, the most hopeful of the three AGI pictures.
S4.quote: I can't stop the machines, but I could help decide who they work for.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Gareth shifts from protecting himself to changing ownership. His distinction between helping him as a worker and as a citizen was the sharpest thought in the interview. He imagines the end as one concrete image: an older colleague's combine driving itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be installing my own replacement and there'd be no time for the politics to catch up. What would help is a robot dividend ready to go, and training paid for by the companies that own the machines. And somewhere for people like Jimmy to go that isn't just a payment, something with a purpose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the pigs think, which sounds like a joke but isn't. A sow's calmer when she knows your voice. I don't know if a robot voice works the same. I'd like someone to find out before they decide.

headlineQuote: A sow's calmer when she knows your voice. I don't know if a robot voice works the same.
portrait: Gareth Garcia is a 27-year-old junior stockman on Fenmoor, a large company-owned arable and pig farm, where he still slips up on farrowing records but is the one everyone calls when the drone won't sync. He is single, rents with a friend, uses AI tools daily, and rarely keeps more than two months' savings. He sees steady change as his chance and is calm about it, but feels guilty about older colleagues like Jimmy, which is why he pushes the union. In the AGI pictures he expects to be kept longest as the machine minder, knows it is temporary, and with more time would retrain, move north and work to change who owns the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would be installing his own replacement with no time for politics to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A robot dividend ready to pay out, training paid for by the companies that own the machines, and purposeful work for older colleagues, not just a payment.
